name: Colin Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Colin. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to tech companies, employers, unions or government. Your name won't be attached to anything, so feel free to say what you'd say in public and also what you really think. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Depends on the season. Right now, November, it's drilling the last of the winter wheat, fixing whatever broke at harvest and moving grain out of the store when the lorries come. I work for the Ashworths on about 900 hectares of wheat, barley and oilseed rape, and I'm the junior of three. In spring and summer I'm mostly on the sprayer, which has GPS steering already, so I spend a lot of hours watching a screen and a boom.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like harvest, even though it's fourteen-hour days, because everyone's in it together and Mrs Ashworth brings pasties out to the field. What wears me out is the money, if I'm honest. My partner Nadia's a care worker and between us we've got about a month's rent saved, and the car's on its last legs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's pretty much where I thought it'd land, to be fair. Lots of noise, a bit of help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say told you so, mainly to my mate Dev who keeps sending me videos of robot tractors. At work I'd say the GPS on the sprayer was the real revolution and that happened ten years ago. Online I'd probably share a meme and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd think, fine, but nothing gets better either. Grain prices still go up and down with the weather in other countries, the Ashworths still pay what they pay, and I still can't see how Nadia and I ever buy a house round here. A flop doesn't fix wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am and keep using the chat thing now and then for spray rules, because it's quicker than the manual. I'd maybe push the Ashworths for the spraying certificate upgrade so I can earn a bit more. And I'd get Nadia to look at joining her care workers' union, because that's where the pay fight actually is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit bored by it, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you use the chat tool for spray rules. What's an example?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last spring I asked it how long you have to leave between spraying a certain herbicide and the rain, because the label print is tiny. It gave me an answer, and I still checked the label, because if I get it wrong it's my certificate on the line. Useful, but I don't trust it with my name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If pay is the real problem, who do you think should fix it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Partly the big buyers, because they squeeze the farmers, and the farmers squeeze us. Partly the government, with a proper minimum for farm work. I don't really blame the Ashworths, they're squeezed too, and they did buy me a new pair of boots when mine split.

S0.say: I'd say told you so, mostly to the friend who keeps sending robot tractor videos. At work I'd say the GPS on the sprayer was the real revolution, years ago.
S0.think: A flop doesn't fix wages. Grain prices still swing, the pay stays the same, and I still can't see how Nadia and I ever buy a house round here.
S0.do: Keeps working as he is and keeps using the AI chat tool now and then for spray rules. Asks his employers to fund a spraying certificate upgrade for slightly better pay, and encourages his partner to join her care workers' union.
S0.feel: Calm, even a little bored by it.
S0.quote: Useful, but I don't trust it with my name.
S0.fieldNote: Colin is matter-of-fact and already uses AI in a careful, double-checking way. In this picture, his real complaint is pay and housing, and he blames buyers and the lack of a proper legal minimum rather than his employers. He thinks of the union fight as happening through his partner's job, not his own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. That one I can actually picture. It's the one I'd bet on, if you asked me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the machines are coming for the driving jobs first, so let's make sure the people who drive get something out of it. At work I'd be the one asking Mr Ashworth if the new kit comes with training. Online I'd share stuff from the farmworkers' union about retraining money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my job is the one that shrinks. A self-driving sprayer doesn't need me sat in it, and on 900 hectares you could run two machines from the office. But somebody has to fill them, fix them, check them and get them out of a ditch, and I'd like that somebody to be me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd wait to see the first robot sprayers on a farm nearby, because I'm not throwing money at something that doesn't work yet. Once I'd seen one working, I'd ask the Ashworths to send me on the dealer's course for it. I'd also do a cheap evening course in farm machinery repairs at the college, about £300, which I'd pay in instalments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but with a plan. Like when the weather forecast says rain at harvest and you've got the drier ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you sure the robot sprayer is proven?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing one do a whole season at Fenwick's, the big farm down the road, without someone walking behind it. And hearing it from their tractor driver, Lee, not the salesman. Lee would tell me if it was rubbish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Nadia say about the £300 course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say do it, and then she'd ask what we're not buying instead. Probably the car gets another year of patching, and we don't go to her sister's wedding abroad, just send a present. That one would hurt a bit.

S1.say: The machines are coming for the driving jobs first, so the people who drive should get something out of it. I'd ask the boss whether the new kit comes with training and share the union's posts about retraining money.
S1.think: My job is the one that shrinks, because a self-driving sprayer doesn't need me in the seat. But someone still has to fill, fix and check the machines, and I want that to be me.
S1.do: Waits to see a robot sprayer work a full season on a nearby farm, then asks his employers to send him on the dealer's course. Pays about £300 in instalments for an evening machinery repair course.
S1.feel: Uneasy, but with a plan, like having the grain drier ready when rain is forecast at harvest.
S1.quote: Somebody has to fill them, fix them, check them and get them out of a ditch, and I'd like that somebody to be me.
S1.fieldNote: This is the picture Colin finds most likely, and he answers it with a steady, step-by-step plan. He needs proof from a peer he trusts, the neighbour's tractor driver, rather than a salesman. The cost lands on his family's plans: skipping a wedding abroad to pay for the course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. So I'd be 29 and the sprayer would drive itself, and fix itself, and... yeah.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the big companies have pulled the rug out from under everyone and the government needs to step in with real money, not a leaflet. At work I'd say it to Mr Ashworth straight: what's the plan for me and Gary and Pete. Online I'd be signing every petition going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What I really think is there's no job for me in two years and no time to get another one. Everything I'd planned in the slow picture, the course and the waiting to see it work, there's no room for. You can't wait for proof when the proof arrives and takes your job the same season.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd stop the car repairs and sell it, and get the bus or borrow Nadia's mum's. I'd sign up with the union, the one for farmworkers, and I'd go to the meetings this time. In the first year after, I'd be leaning on whatever government support there is, and hoping Nadia's care work holds out a bit longer, because people still want a human holding their hand, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My stomach drops just saying it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Nadia's work might hold out. Do you believe that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I want to. Her job is helping old people wash and eat and talk. I'd like to think nobody wants a robot doing that to their gran. But the card says robots do hands-on work too, so honestly, I don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the first thing you'd cut, money-wise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car, like I said, and then the phone contract down to the cheapest one. Then food gets boring: rice, lentils, the reduced shelf. We've done it before, the winter Nadia was off with her back, so we know how.

S2.say: The big companies have pulled the rug from under everyone and the government has to step in with real money, not a leaflet. I'd ask the boss straight what the plan is for the three of us, and sign every petition.
S2.think: There's no job for me in two years and no time to find another. My usual plan, wait for proof and then retrain, has no room to work.
S2.do: Sells the car and cuts the phone and food bills straight away. Joins the farmworkers' union and goes to meetings, then relies on government support and his partner's care work in the first year after.
S2.feel: Alarmed, with his stomach dropping as he says it.
S2.quote: You can't wait for proof when the proof arrives and takes your job the same season.
S2.fieldNote: The two-year picture breaks Colin's usual way of dealing with change, which is to wait for proof and then follow. He knows this, and says it clearly. He pins his hope on his partner's care work but is honest that the card doesn't protect it, and he falls back on cost cutting they already practised in a hard winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay. That's a bit better, but not loads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years to set up a proper safety net, so let's not waste three of them arguing. At work I'd say let's be first round here to try the new machines, not last, so we know how they work. Online I'd share the union's plans for retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years is enough for me to see the machines arrive before they take everything. I'd get two or three years of being the guy who looks after them. After that I'm not sure what's left, because the card says the AI can do almost anything, so the robot sprayer won't need a minder for long either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd do the machinery repair course and get on the dealer's training as soon as the first robot sprayers came out. I'd try to save £100 a month, which is a lot for us. By year three I'd be asking the union and the college what jobs are actually left when the machines look after themselves, and I'd follow whatever most of my mates are doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's like the start of a long uphill walk where you can't see the top.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd follow your mates. What if they're all waiting too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha, then we're all stood in a field waiting. That's fair. Probably I'd follow Dev, he's always first. If he moved into something and it worked out, I'd go after him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the government to do with the five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pay people to learn while they still have a job, not after. And something like a wage for people the machines replace, paid for by whoever owns the machines. That's what I'd vote for.

S3.say: We've got five years to build a proper safety net, so let's not waste three of them arguing. At work I'd push for us to try the new machines first, so we know how they work.
S3.think: Five years lets me see the machines arrive before they take everything, and gives me two or three years as their minder. After that I'm not sure anything is left, because the robots won't need a minder for long.
S3.do: Takes the machinery repair course and the dealer's training on the first robot sprayers in year one. Tries to save £100 a month and, by year three, asks the union and college which jobs remain, following his most adventurous friend.
S3.feel: Anxious, like starting a long uphill walk without seeing the top.
S3.quote: Ha, then we're all stood in a field waiting.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives Colin enough time to use his usual follow-once-proven approach, but he sees that it only buys a few years. He laughed when the gap was named: if everyone waits, nobody moves first. His political wishes are specific: paid learning while still employed, and support funded by machine owners.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be 37. Kids, maybe, by then. That changes how I think about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a proper amount of time and there's no excuse for anyone to get left behind. I'd be telling the younger lads on the farm to learn the machines now. Online I'd be calmer than in the other ones, sharing the useful stuff rather than the angry stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years means I could have a whole second career before it hits. But it also means Nadia and I would be deciding about kids in the middle of it. I'd want to know there's a world for them before we start, and I don't know if I would know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the first two years on the machinery course and the robot training, and get paid a bit more for it. Then by year four or five I'd look at moving to something the machines reach last, maybe electrician, because someone has to wire all this up. We'd save properly and probably wait on kids until we could see where it was going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not panicky. There's time to think, which is kind of its own worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said waiting on kids. Is that a real conversation you two would have?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's already a conversation, to be honest, just about money. This would make it about the future too. Nadia would say we can't wait forever for the world to be sorted, and she'd be right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why electrician?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the robots still plug into something, at least for a while, and my uncle's an electrician and he's never short of work. It's a three-year course and I'd want to see a few others do it first, but with ten years I could.

S4.say: Ten years is a proper amount of time, so nobody should get left behind. I'd tell the younger lads to learn the machines now, and share the useful stuff online rather than the angry stuff.
S4.think: Ten years means I could have a whole second career before it hits. But Nadia and I would be deciding about kids in the middle of it, and I'd want to know there's a world for them first.
S4.do: Spends the first two years on machinery and robot training, then moves toward electrical training by year four or five. Saves steadily and delays having children until the future is clearer.
S4.feel: Uneasy but not panicked, finding that having time to think is its own kind of worry.
S4.quote: Nadia would say we can't wait forever for the world to be sorted, and she'd be right.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years shifts Colin's concern from his job to whether to start a family. His career plan is a steady progression, from machine minder to electrician, guided by an uncle who's never short of work. He still wants to see others go first, but with ten years he thinks he can afford to watch and then follow.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Everything I know how to do, waiting and watching and then following, doesn't work if it's that quick. What would help is money for people to learn new jobs while they're still in work, and the union being strong enough that the Ashworths and farms like them have to talk to us before the machines arrive.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what my partner does. Everyone asks about farming, but in our house the real question is whether Nadia's job is safe, because if hers goes as well, then we're both done. I'd like someone to ask the care workers.

headlineQuote: You can't wait for proof when the proof arrives and takes your job the same season.
portrait: Colin Varga is 27 and the junior of three workers on a 900-hectare grain and oilseed farm, mostly driving the sprayer. He and his partner Nadia, a care worker, have about a month's rent saved. He uses AI tools now and then but always checks them, and his way with change is to wait for proof from someone he trusts and then follow. That works in the AI Plateau and Steady Disruption pictures and breaks down in AGI by 2028, when there's no time for proof. With five or ten years he sketches a path from machine minder to electrician, and the longer warning turns his worry toward whether to have children.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because his habit of waiting for proof and then following has no time to work.
whatWouldHelp: Paid training while people are still employed, and a strong union so farms must talk to workers before machines arrive.
